name: Reflexion

paper.title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning

construction.unit: self-reflection: a few sentences of text written after a failed trial
construction.kept_as: LLM-written diagnosis of the failure and a plan for the next attempt
construction.processing: after a failed trial the reflection LLM reads the trajectory (and, in ALFWorld, earlier reflections) and writes what went wrong and what to do instead
construction.writer: reflection LLM, prompted with 2 few-shot reflections (same model family as the actor)

organization.structure: per-task list of reflections (long-term) next to the current trajectory (short-term)
organization.stores: one reflection list per task; the running trajectory

management.operations: append each new reflection; keep only the most recent Ω
management.forgetting: sliding window: reflections older than the last Ω drop out (Ω = 3 ALFWorld and HotPotQA, 1 programming)

retrieval.candidates: every kept reflection of the current task
retrieval.selection: the last Ω by recency; no search or ranking

use.context: few-shot examples + reflections + task + current trajectory in the actor prompt
use.reasoning: ReAct or CoT actor; the task is retried until solved or the trial budget runs out

classify.note: Memory is a short list per task; all kept reflections go into the prompt. The only management is the sliding window of Ω entries.

stages.ingestion: Each trial produces a trajectory of actions and observations (short-term memory); an evaluator turns it into a reward: exact match on HotPotQA, a hand-written heuristic or an LLM classifier on ALFWorld, self-written unit tests for code.
stages.construction: After a failed trial a reflection LLM, prompted with two example reflections, writes a few sentences diagnosing the failure and proposing a new plan.
stages.organization: Reflections are appended to a list kept for that task only; there is no index and no sharing across tasks.
stages.update: The list is bounded to the last Ω reflections (Ω = 3 for ALFWorld and HotPotQA, 1 for programming).
stages.retrieval: No search: every kept reflection of the task is placed in the actor prompt of the next trial.
stages.answer: The actor (ReAct or CoT; for code, an implementation generator) reads few-shot examples, the reflections, the task and its current trajectory.
stages.learning: Called 'verbal reinforcement learning': behaviour changes across trials only through the reflection text; no weights are updated.

summary: An agent retries a task and, after each failure, writes a short self-reflection that is kept in a per-task sliding-window memory (last 1-3 reflections) and prepended to the next attempt's prompt.

headline: Memory is a handful of LLM-written reflections about one task; it is never searched and never shared with other tasks.
The benefit shows up across repeated attempts at the same task, and each retry is triggered by an evaluator (on HotPotQA, exact match against the gold answer).

The EPM ablation (Fig. 4c) is reported only as a curve and an '8% absolute' gap, on CoT with gold context.

text: Nothing is searched: all kept reflections of the task are written into the actor prompt, between the few-shot examples and the task.
The actor then steps through the environment with its trajectory as short-term memory until it finishes or hits the step cap.

discussion.takeaway: Turning a pass/fail signal into a short written lesson, and showing the last few lessons on the next attempt, lets an LLM agent improve on the same task over trials without any weight updates.

claims.evidence: ALFWorld: 130 of 134 tasks solved with the heuristic evaluator over 12 trials; ReAct alone plateaus after trial 6-7 (§4.1, Fig. 3).
HotPotQA (100 q): ReAct 0.30 → 0.55 and CoT (GT) 0.60 → 0.77 with text-davinci-003 (Table 5); baselines solve no new question after trial 1 (§4.2).

claims.claim: Verbal reflection beats just showing the last trajectory.
claims.evidence: About 8 points above the episodic-memory (last trajectory) baseline on CoT (GT) (§4.2, Fig. 4c).

claims.claim: State of the art on code generation.
claims.evidence: HumanEval Python pass@1 91.0 vs 80.1 for GPT-4 (Table 1); MBPP Python is the exception (77.1 vs 80.1), linked to a 16.3% false-positive rate of self-generated tests (Table 2).

claims.claim: Both test generation and self-reflection are needed.
claims.evidence: HumanEval Rust hardest 50: 68 full vs 52 without tests and 60 without reflection (Table 3).

limits: Policy optimisation in language can still get stuck in local minima; on WebShop it did not improve after 4 trials (App. B.1).
Long-term memory is only a sliding window with a maximum size.
Test-driven code feedback struggles with non-deterministic, impure, hardware-dependent or concurrent functions.
Self-correction appears only with stronger models: starchat-beta gains nothing (App. A, Table 4).
reading: Memory never leaves the task: each environment or question keeps its own list, so the results measure improvement on repeated attempts, not transfer to new tasks.
On HotPotQA the between-trial signal is exact match against the gold answer, so the agent knows when it is wrong; accuracy after several trials is not comparable with single-attempt QA.
The HotPotQA code does not enforce the 3-reflection bound stated in the paper, and the ALFWorld code stops trials on a different rule than the one described (see paper vs code).
Table 1 does not name the model behind the Reflexion column; only Table 3 states GPT-4 as the base model (HumanEval Rust).
Most ALFWorld and HotPotQA numbers are shown only as curves (Fig. 3-4); the text gives 130/134 and the 22%/20% improvements.

abstract.text: Reflexion lets a language agent learn from trial and error without fine-tuning. After each attempt an evaluator gives a scalar or binary signal, and a second LLM turns a failure into a short written self-reflection. These reflections are kept in a small episodic buffer and added to the prompt of the next attempt at the same task. The authors report gains on ALFWorld, HotPotQA and code generation, including 91% pass@1 on HumanEval, and analyse which kinds of feedback and components matter.
